title: CNC Machining: Works and Manufacturing Process
summary: Get a better understanding of the inner workings behind this important manufacturing process.
body_text: 1. Turning in Machining Processes Turning is used to shape cylindrical parts by rotating the workpiece against a cutting tool. The process is widely employed in industries like automotive and aerospace for producing shafts, pistons, and other rotational parts. Turning offers high precision and smooth finishes, making it ideal for components with rotational symmetry. Turning is essential for creating high-quality parts in turning machining processes . 2. Milling in Machining Processes Milling is used to remove material from a workpiece using rotating cutters. It is ideal for creating complex shapes such as brackets, slots, and pockets in materials like metal, plastic, and composites. Milling provides high accuracy, which makes it vital for industries like automotive, aerospace, and electronics. Milling is key in producing intricate parts in milling machining processes . 3. Drilling in Machining Processes Drilling is used to create round holes in a workpiece with a rotating drill bit. It is a fundamental operation in industries like construction, automotive, and aerospace for making holes in materials such as metal, plastic, and wood. Drilling allows for precise hole placement and depth control, making it crucial for parts requiring accuracy. Drilling is essential for creating holes in drilling machining processes . 4. Grinding in Machining Processes Grinding is used to achieve fine surface finishes and high precision on a workpiece using an abrasive wheel. It is widely applied in industries like automotive, aerospace, and tooling for finishing metal parts and improving surface quality. Grinding allows for tight tolerances and smooth surfaces, making it crucial for high-quality parts. Grinding is important for surface finishing in grinding machining processes . 5. Boring in Machining Processes Boring is used to enlarge an existing hole in a workpiece with a single-point cutting tool. It is often used for producing large, precise holes in engine blocks, machine housings, and other industrial components. Boring improves hole diameter accuracy and surface finish, ensuring higher precision. Boring is key for hole enlargement in boring machining processes . 6. Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) EDM is used to remove material from a workpiece by using electrical discharges to erode the material. It is effective for machining hard metals and intricate shapes that are difficult to work with using traditional cutting tools. EDM provides high precision and is ideal for creating complex molds, cavities, and fine details. EDM is essential for precise cutting in EDM machining processes . 7. Laser Cutting in Machining Processes Laser cutting is used to cut, engrave, or etch materials using a focused laser beam. It is applied in industries like automotive, aerospace, and electronics for making precise cuts in metals, plastics, and wood. Laser cutting offers clean edges with minimal heat-affected zones, making it essential for intricate designs and shapes. Laser cutting is crucial for producing high-precision components in laser cutting machining processes . 8. Plasma Cutting in Machining Processes Plasma cutting is used to cut through conductive materials like steel, aluminum, and brass with a plasma torch. It is commonly used in industries like construction, automotive, and manufacturing for large-scale cutting tasks. Plasma cutting provides fast, efficient cutting for thick conductive materials where standard industrial tolerances are acceptable. Plasma cutting is vital for high-speed cutting in plasma cutting machining processes . 9. Waterjet Cutting in Machining Processes Waterjet cutting is used to cut materials using a high-pressure stream of water, often with abrasive particles. It is used for cutting materials like metals, glass, and ceramics without generating heat-affected zones. Waterjet cutting provides precise cuts and is ideal for intricate designs and complex shapes. Waterjet cutting is important for delicate materials in waterjet cutting machining processes . 10. Tapping in Machining Processes Tapping is used to create internal threads in a workpiece with a rotating tool that either cuts or displaces material to form the thread profile. It is commonly used in industries like automotive and manufacturing for producing threaded holes in components that will later be assembled. Tapping is crucial for creating strong, reliable threaded connections. Tapping is essential for thread creation in tapping machining processes . 11. Broaching in Machining Processes Broaching is used to remove material with a tool that has multiple teeth, enabling high-efficiency cutting. It is widely used in industries like automotive and aerospace for producing precise shapes such as gears, keyways, and splines. Broaching allows for the rapid production of complex shapes with high accuracy. Broaching is important for intricate shapes in broaching machining processes. 12. Swiss Machining in Machining Processes Swiss machining is used to manufacture small, high-precision parts using a sliding headstock to feed the workpiece into the cutting tool. It is widely used in industries like medical device manufacturing and watchmaking for creating tiny, intricate components. Swiss machining offers extreme precision and the ability to achieve tight tolerances on small parts. Swiss machining is essential for high-precision components in Swiss machining processes . How Does CNC Machining Compare to Manual Machining? CNC machining compares to manual machining through the automation of the cutting process and the removal of human error from the production cycle. Computers execute the programmed instructions without fatigue or loss of concentration. Human operators guide the tool path in manual processes through sight and physical feedback. CNC machines maintain 24 hours of continuous production with a high level of accuracy. Manual machines require constant human attention for every individual cut performed on the workpiece. Repeatability increases with automation because the software runs the exact same code every single time. Manual outcomes vary because human skill levels change throughout a long shift. Precision levels in automated environments commonly reach 0.005 mm to 0.01 mm. Manual precision depends on the steadiness of the human hand and the quality of the visual scales. Manual machining stays useful for simple repairs (fixing a single shaft) or basic mechanical parts. Setups for manual lathes require less time for simple shapes like bolts. Automated setups involve digital design and G-code generation. Large production runs favor computers to reduce labor costs and increase speed. Manual shops focus on prototyping, where designs change quickly between parts. Training for automation focuses on computer logic and software operation. Manual training emphasizes mechanical intuition and tactile feedback from the machinery. Industry leaders evaluate the differences in output to determine the best factory strategy. Choices between automated and hand-operated equipment impact total factory speed and reliability. Manufacturers analyze CNC Machining vs Manual Machining . What Are the Advantages of CNC Over Manual Machining? The advantages of CNC over Manual Machining are listed below. Higher Precision : CNC machines follow exact programmed coordinates during each operation. The system maintains tight tolerances across large production batches. Each cycle repeats the same measurements without deviation. The process eliminates variation caused by manual positioning and hand adjustments. Greater Production Speed : CNC machines execute cutting paths without pauses for manual recalculation. Automated tool changes reduce downtime between operations. Continuous cycles keep production moving for long periods. Shops complete more parts within the same timeframe. Improved Consistency : CNC programs repeat identical toolpaths for every unit produced. Each finished part matches the original design specifications. Production quality stays stable across short and long runs. The process removes inconsistency linked to operator fatigue or shifting technique. Reduced Human Error : Computer-guided instructions control feed rates, depth of cut, and positioning. The system prevents common mistakes from manual measurement or alignment. Fewer errors reduce scrap and rework. Production flows with fewer interruptions caused by corrections. Complex Part Capability : CNC machines manage multi-axis movement during machining. The system produces intricate shapes and detailed contours with accuracy. Internal cavities and compound angles stay aligned with the digital model. Manufacturers expand design possibilities beyond manual limits. Better Material Utilization : CNC software calculates efficient cutting paths before production begins. The process limits unnecessary material removal. Controlled machining reduces scrap rates. Shops manage raw material usage with greater efficiency. Lower Labor Intensity : Operators focus on setup and monitoring instead of constant manual control. The machine performs repetitive cutting motions without fatigue. Labor shifts toward programming and inspection tasks. Production relies less on continuous physical effort. Safer Operation : Enclosed machine designs contain chips and debris during cutting. Automated cycles reduce direct exposure to rotating tools. Operators interact with control panels instead of active cutting zones. Work environments maintain higher safety standards through controlled operation. Is CNC Machining More Accurate Than Manual Machining? CNC machining provides higher accuracy than manual machining, so the answer to the question is yes. Computers eliminate the risk of human error during the cutting process by following digital instructions. Sensors monitor tool positions 100 times per second to verify the position against the digital blueprint. The use of high-precision ball screws and backlash compensation software maintains tight tolerances that manual equipment fails to provide. Human eyes struggle to detect deviations smaller than 0.1 millimeters during a manual cut. CNC spindles reach 20000 rotations per minute with high dynamic stability and managed thermal expansion. Manual operators rely on visual scales and hand-cranked dials for every measurement. Thermal expansion in the cutting tools is managed through automated cooling systems in modern CNC units. Manual processes result in slight variations between identical parts due to the inconsistency of human movement. Programmed paths follow mathematical coordinates with zero deviation. Medical devices (implants) require the high precision of automation to ensure patient safety. Aerospace components (turbine blades) demand accuracy levels that manual methods fail to reach. Digital feedback loops correct the tool path instantly if a deviation is detected. Human fatigue leads to errors during long shifts in a manual workshop. Automated machines execute the same commands for 1000 parts without any variance. Numerical control allows modern factories to meet the tight engineering standards required for high-tech components. Accuracy remains the primary differentiator for high-quality industrial production. What Types of Holes Can CNC Machines Produce? Types of holes can CNC machine produces are listed below. Through Hole : A cutting tool drills completely through the material from one side to the other. The hole allows fasteners or shafts to pass entirely through a part. Machinists use through holes in structural frames and mechanical assemblies. CNC control keeps the diameter and alignment consistent across multiple parts. Blind Hole : A drill or end mill cuts into the material without breaking through the opposite side. The bottom of the hole stops at a specified depth. Designers use blind holes for threaded fasteners and mounting points. CNC programming controls depth precisely to match design requirements. Tapped Hole : A tap tool cuts internal threads inside a drilled hole. The threads hold bolts or screws securely in place. Engineers include tapped holes among common types of holes in engineering for fastening systems. CNC machines synchronize spindle speed and feed rate to cut clean threads. Counterbore Hole : A larger diameter recess cuts into the top portion of a drilled hole. The recess allows a bolt head or socket cap screw to sit flush with the surface. Machinists create the smaller pilot hole first, then enlarge the upper section. CNC positioning keeps both diameters concentric. Countersink Hole : A conical cutting tool shapes the top of a drilled hole into an angled profile. The angled opening fits flat-head screws. The process ensures the fastener sits level with the material surface. CNC control maintains uniform angle and depth across production runs. Reamed Hole : A reamer tool refines a previously drilled hole to a precise diameter. The tool removes a small amount of material to improve surface finish and tolerance. Engineers rely on reamed holes for tight-fitting pins and dowels. CNC machines guide the reamer straight through the bore for accurate sizing. Spotface Hole : A cutting tool machines a flat circular surface around a hole opening. The flat area provides a smooth seating surface for washers or bolt heads. Machinists apply spotfacing when rough surfaces prevent proper fastening. CNC machines position the tool accurately over each hole location. Tapered Hole : A tapered cutting tool creates a hole with a gradual change in diameter. The shape supports tapered pins or specialized fittings. Designers include tapered profiles among advanced types of holes in engineering . CNC control manages the angle and depth to meet design specifications. How Are Tapped and Countersunk Holes Made? Tapped and countersunk holes are made using specialized bits guided by numerical control to ensure a precise fit for fasteners. Threading tools cut internal grooves for screws, while countersunk holes use angled bits to create a conical opening. The process starts with a pilot hole drilled to a specific diameter. Tapping requires a precise rotation-to-feed ratio to avoid breaking the tool inside the material. Countersinking involves a specialized tool, commonly 82, 90, or 100 degrees, to bevel the top of the hole opening. Screws sit flush with the surface after a countersink operation is completed. CNC controllers manage the spindle speed and depth for types of hole geometries. Automated tool changers switch from the drill bit to the countersink bit in a few seconds. Synchronization between the spindle and the Z-axis ensures accurate thread pitch compliant with standard thread classes in every tapped hole. Manual tapping involves a hand wrench and constant reverse turns to clear metal debris. Automated systems use rigid tapping to increase speed and prevent tool failure. Countersink depths are maintained within 0.05 millimeters across a large batch of parts. Fasteners require specific geometries for proper assembly of mechanical components. Engineers specify the hole dimensions in the digital design (bolt diameter). Automated machining ensures consistency in mass-produced assemblies used in vehicles and appliances. Precision is maintained by the computer throughout the drilling and threading sequence. Can CNC Machines Create Precision Holes? CNC machines create precision holes with a high level of accuracy, which means the answer to the question is yes. High-speed spindles and rigid tool holders allow the equipment to meet tight tolerances. Hole diameters are maintained within 0.01 millimeters using reaming or precision boring operations following the initial drilling. Reaming operations follow the initial drilling to achieve a mirror-like surface finish inside the hole. Automated centering tools ensure the hole location stays exact on the X and Y axes. Deep hole drilling utilizes peck cycles to clear metal chips and prevent heat buildup. Calibration of the machine axes happens before production to verify mathematical accuracy. Aerospace parts (engine housings) require thousands of precision holes for cooling and fastening. Medical devices (bone plates) feature tiny holes with high precision internal finishes. Manual drilling lacks the rigidity to keep the hole perfectly perpendicular to the material surface. Automation calculates the optimal speed for every specific material (aluminum or titanium). Tool wear sensors alert the operator if the drill bit becomes dull during the process. Precision boring heads allow for micro-adjustments to the diameter of the hole. Consistency across 500 parts is guaranteed by the digital code stored in the machine. Industries rely on automated drilling for high-performance components used in critical systems. The computer manages the entire sequence to ensure the holes meet engineering specifications. What Materials Can Be Used in CNC Machining? Materials that are used in CNC machining include a wide range of metals (aluminum and steel) and high-performance plastics (Delrin and Nylon). Aluminum remains the frequent metal choice due to its high machinability and low weight. Steel alloys (304 stainless) provide high strength for heavy industrial parts. Titanium is machined for aerospace and medical uses because of its biocompatibility. Plastics (Nylon or Delrin) are carved into gears and mechanical housings. Cutting tools are selected based on the hardness of the specific material being shaped. Hardened steels require cubic boron nitride (CBN) or ceramic cutters to achieve a clean finish. Heat management is necessary when machining plastics to prevent the material from melting. Softwoods and hardwoods are shaped into furniture components using high-speed routers. Carbon fiber composites are machined using specialized dust collection and sealed electronics to protect the operator and prevent electrical short-circuiting of the equipment. Brass and copper are chosen for electrical components due to their high conductivity. Material properties (density or melting point) dictate the spindle speed and feed rate. Lubricants are applied during metal cutting to reduce friction and tool wear. Scrap material is recycled in industrial settings to save production costs. Manufacturing needs drive the selection of different raw stocks to meet the specific requirements of the final product. Every material is processed according to a digital blueprint to ensure the final dimensions are accurate. How Do CNC Machines Cut Metals and Plastics? CNC machines cut metals and plastics by using a spinning tool to shear away chips according to a digital blueprint. Milling bits remove material from the surface through physical shearing at high speeds. Lasers vaporize material to create intricate designs in thin sheets of metal or acrylic. Metal cutting requires high torque to overcome the bond of the atoms in the material. Plastics are carved at higher feed rates to minimize the contact time of the hot tool. Cooling fluids wash away metal chips to prevent the tool from clogging or breaking. Vacuum tables hold plastic sheets in place during routing operations to ensure stability. Spindle speeds for aluminum reach 15000 rotations per minute for a smooth finish. Steel machining uses lower speeds to prevent tool burn and overheating. Computer code manages the tool path to ensure the cutter does not dwell in one spot too long. Excessive heat distorts the shape of plastic parts during the manufacturing process. Carbide tools maintain a sharp edge even when cutting hardened metals like titanium. Finished parts feature smooth surfaces without the need for manual sanding. Precision removal of material follows the digital path exactly as programmed. Factories use the methods to produce durable components for the automotive and electronics industries. Is Aluminum Commonly Used in CNC Machining? Aluminum is a frequent material in CNC machining due to its excellent strength-to-weight ratio, so the answer is yes. The metal exhibits high thermal conductivity, which helps dissipate heat during high-speed milling. Many aluminum alloys exhibit high machinability, though proper chip-breaker geometry is required to prevent "gummy" alloys from wrapping around the tool. Surface finishes on aluminum parts appear mirror-like straight from the machine. Automotive manufacturers use aluminum for engine blocks and suspension parts to reduce vehicle weight. Aerospace engineers choose the metal for wing spars and fuselage frames because it is lightweight. Aluminum alloys (6061 or 7075) are readily available and affordable for most projects. Anodizing processes adhere well to the metal to provide corrosion resistance and color. Machining aluminum consumes less energy than cutting steel or hardened titanium. Electronic housings utilize the non-magnetic properties of the metal to protect internal circuits. Fast production cycles make aluminum the favorite for prototyping new designs. While aluminum is structurally stable, internal residual stresses can lead to warping during material removal if proper machining sequences are not followed. Recycling aluminum scrap recovers 95 percent of the energy used in initial production. Industry demand for the metal stays high in automated workshops because it is easy to process. Manufacturers prefer the material for high-volume part production. What are the Applications of CNC Machining? The applications of CNC Machining are listed below. Aerospace Industry : Aerospace manufacturers machine structural frames, engine parts, and landing gear components while maintaining strict material traceability and quality standards. The process maintains strict dimensional accuracy for flight safety. Complex geometries and lightweight materials demand multi-axis capability. CNC systems produce repeatable parts that meet regulatory standards. Automotive Industry : Automotive companies machine engine blocks, transmission housings, and brake components. The process supports high-volume production with consistent quality. Precision machining ensures a proper fit between moving parts. CNC equipment keeps production cycles efficient and controlled. Medical Industry : Medical manufacturers produce surgical instruments and implant components, achieving specific surface roughness (Ra) values required for biocompatibility and sterilization. The process holds tight tolerances required for human body applications. Clean surface finishes support hygiene and sterilization standards. CNC systems create custom implants based on digital models. Electronics Industry : Electronics companies machine heat sinks, enclosures, and connector components, often incorporating integrated EMI/RFI shielding features. The process shapes aluminum and copper parts for thermal control. Precise cutting ensures proper alignment of internal assemblies. CNC machining supports compact and detailed product designs. Defense Industry : Defense contractors machine firearm components, vehicle parts, and communication hardware. The process maintains dimensional consistency across production batches. Strong materials require accurate cutting parameters and stable toolpaths. CNC systems meet strict performance and reliability standards. Energy Sector : Energy companies machine turbine blades from nickel-based superalloys, pump housings, and drilling components using advanced 5-axis strategies. The process handles heavy-duty materials used in power generation and oil extraction. Precision machining ensures proper sealing and rotation of mechanical systems. CNC equipment supports both renewable and conventional energy projects. Industrial Equipment Manufacturing : Industrial manufacturers produce gears, shafts, and machine frames through CNC machining. The process ensures accurate alignment between mechanical assemblies. Durable metal components require stable cutting operations. CNC systems support both custom fabrication and repeat production runs. Prototyping and Product Development : Engineering teams create functional prototypes using CNC machining. The process converts digital CAD models into physical parts quickly. Designers test fit, strength, and performance before mass production. CNC systems shorten development cycles and support design revisions. 1. Automotive Industry CNC machining is widely used in the automotive industry to produce precise engine blocks, cylinder heads, and transmission housings. The technology ensures high accuracy, making it ideal for manufacturing vehicle parts with tight tolerances. CNC machines enable the production of large quantities of parts efficiently, meeting the high demand in the automotive sector. The precision and reliability offered by CNC machining make it essential for maintaining consistent quality in automotive manufacturing.

title: ESG na indústria farmacêutica: quais as medidas do setor para incluir práticas socioambientais?
summary: Entenda como funciona hoje a inclusão de ESG na indústria farmacêutica e saiba o que deve ser feito para melhorar
body_text: Iniciativas ESG na indústria farmacêutica têm sido cada vez mais promissoras para diminuir os descartes impróprios de objetos perigosos. O fator é preocupante, em vista de um setor que fatura R$66 bilhões por ano , como relata a Associação Brasileira de Redes de Farmácias de Drogarias (Abrafarma). As políticas ESG envolvem interferências ambientais, sociais e de governança, cujo objetivo é minimizar o impacto na natureza , além de produzir tratamentos mais alcançáveis para a população. A PWC, aponta os impactos da presença ou da falta de implementações do modelo ESG no mercado, e como eles afetam toda a cadeia produtiva, principalmente quando se trata de fortalecer os investimentos. De acordo com a mais recente pesquisa global feita com investidores, em 2021, a empresa constatou que: 79% consideram os riscos e as oportunidades ESG um fator importante na decisão de investimento; 49% se desfazem do investimento se a empresa não tomasse ações para tratar as questões ESG; 33% acreditam que a qualidade dos relatórios ESG atuais, em média, é boa. Ou seja, adotar medidas de ESG ainda é um processo que caminha em passos curtos, porém, qualquer movimento se torna relevante para a mudança de hábito nas corporações. Especificamente, neste artigo vamos abordar como funciona o modelo ESG na indústria farmacêutica. Você vai saber o conceito, os desafios, a importância, e muito mais. Continue com a gente! O que é ESG? ESG refere-se a environmental, social and governance , que, traduzido para o português, significa meio ambiente, sociedade e governança corporativa. O**“E”** da sigla está relacionado a medidas ambientais. A mudança climática é o maior objetivo dos investidores, que se preocupam com as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, qualidade do ar e o gerenciamento da água. O**“S”** refere-se às medidas sociais. Inserido na década de 60, o movimento dos Direitos Civis e da Guerra do Vietnã contribuiu para começar as ações socialmente responsáveis. Em 2020, quando surgiu o movimento Black Lives Matter , a sociedade mundial mostrou-se preocupada com a falta de inclusão social, principalmente em razão dos grupos raciais e étnicos minoritários. Nesse sentido, as empresas farmacêuticas se mostraram presentes na luta diária contra as desigualdades raciais, violência policial e racismo sistêmico, como também em uma relação sólida e transparente com a cadeia de fornecedores. Leia o nosso ebook de Programa de Diversidade de Fornecedores e entenda qual o melhor caminho que uma empresa brasileira deve trilhar para implementar um programa de diversidade de fornecedores de sucesso em nosso País. Por fim, o “G” em ESG, ou governança, diz respeito às políticas de gestão da companhia . Estão inseridos nesse aspecto, pessoas que atuam em conselhos, interessados em prevenir contra práticas ilegais, como fraudes e subornos ( compliance ), e fortalecer a transparência e honestidade dentro das corporações. Principal desafio de implantação de ESG na Indústria Farmacêutica O interesse em agregar aspectos ESG só aumenta, principalmente quando se trata do maior problema aparente: o preço dos medicamentos. Isso interfere nas avaliações ESG, pois dificulta a acessibilidade aos produtos. Uma política ampla de subsídios para remédios está longe de ser prioridade da agenda brasileira. Entre baixas e altas, o País sofre uma média de reajuste de 11% , como constata o Sindusfarma . Embora exista um programa de subsídios de medicamentos pelo Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), por sua vez, este é um processo lento, uma vez que a lista é restrita e nem sempre contempla as terapias indicadas para a população. Medidas para implementar o ESG na indústria farmacêutica O Health Research Institute (HRI) , da PwC, analisou as iniciativas ESG de 32 empresas farmacêuticas e de biociências e descobriu que o setor poderia obter benefícios adicionais ao incorporar também um enfoque ambiental e de governança em sua estratégia geral. Conforme a pesquisa, os esforços ESG na indústria farmacêutica e de biociências devem ser: Ambiental Frota de veículos sustentáveis; Neutralidade de carbono em 5 a 10 anos; Gestão avançada de resíduos e redução de custos de fabricação por meio de investimento em fabricação contínua ou outras tecnologias. Social Contribuições financeiras significativas para medicamentos e terapias acessíveis a comunidades carentes; Adoção e incorporação precoce de diversidade em ensaios clínicos para pesquisa e desenvolvimento Resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos baseada na diversidade de fornecedores e em avaliação de riscos; Esforços para melhorar a segurança do produto; Programas abrangentes de D&I (diversidade e inclusão) , voltados ao recrutamento e mentoria. Governança Relatório abrangente de responsabilidade social corporativa para monitorar e compartilhar o progresso mensurável em ESG; Nomeação de liderança ESG; Diversidade de gênero e raça nos conselhos de administração; Metas de equidade salarial ; Políticas de ética, compliance e fraude. Quais as principais formas de descarte ideais? Um ponto importante sobre a sustentabilidade hospitalar é em relação à produção de lixo nos hospitais e clínicas , o que leva à aplicação de ESG na indústria farmacêutica para incentivar ações de armazenamento, retirada e coleta de resíduos a fim de evitar contaminações. Além de realizar o descarte de forma segura, ao adotar medidas ESG, os hospitais se conscientizam sobre os possíveis acidentes com os EPIs (Equipamentos de Proteção Individuais) . Nesse sentido, são incluídas medidas para averiguar a durabilidade dos equipamentos, como prevenir imprevistos e prezar pela qualidade. A importância de implementar o ESG na indústria farmacêutica O comprador do passado é aquele que acredita que governança e compliance em compras não são relevantes. Ele não os valoriza porque crê que o investimento não vale a pena e só traz burocracia. Já o comprador do futuro abraça temas como causas ambientais, justiça e igualdade como valores pessoais. Ele é um agente transformador desta prática e realidade dentro do seu ambiente profissional. Em meio às mudanças no setor farmacêutico a partir da pandemia, vale a pena inserir um modelo de sustentabilidade, governança e social neste ramo. title: Oscilloscope Testing of 10Base-T1S Automotive Ethernet Signal Integrity
summary: Figure 1. The 10Base-T1S TDME option features easy eye diagram creation for signal integrity analysis. Click on any image to enlarge it. In addition to special serial data bus measurements of 10Base-T1S signals, the 10Base-T1S Trigger, Decode, Measure/Graph & Eye Diagram (TDME) option automates the generation and display of eye diagrams on Teledyne LeCroy oscilloscopes. Eye diagrams are an important element of serial data analysis, used to understand the signal integrity of the communications network. The eye diagram is a general-purpose tool for analyzing serial digital communications signals. It shows the effects of additive vertical noise, horizontal jitter, duty cycle distortion, inter-symbol interference, and crosstalk on a serial data stream. The eye diagram is formed by overlaying repetitive occurrences of slightly more than a single clock period (UI) of a serial data signal on a persistence display which shows the accumulated history of multiple acquisitions, as shown in Figure 1. Due to the use of Differential Manchester encoding (DME), the 10Base-T1S eye is formed with twice the signal clock rate. The signal shown has a symbol rate of 12.5 Mbps and the eye is clocked at 25 Mbps. DME is a bipolar encoding scheme where a logical one is represented by transition (of either polarity) in the middle of a bit period. A logical zero is represented by the absence of a transition during the middle of a bit period. DME encoding is illustrated in Figure 2. Figure 2. Differential Manchester (DME) encoding used in 10Base-T1S. DME uses a transition of either polarity during the middle of a bit period to indicate a logical 1 and the lack of a transition to signal a logical 0. The vertical blue dotted lines indicate the bit periods. The logical 1 signals break the bit period in half, so evaluating the eye requires the double symbol rate. Figure 3. An annotated view of the 10Base-T1S eye diagram showing the significant eye parameters. Based on this information we can take a closer look at the 10Base-T1S eye diagram shown in Figure 3. The bit period is 40 ns corresponding to the bit rate of 25 Mbps. This is the effective symbol rate for the DME signal. The data source for the eye diagram can be user selected to be the entire acquisition or a zoom of a selected data packet. There are several measurement parameters that help characterize eye diagrams: Zero Level - The mean value of the logical 0 level of the eye diagram. One Level - The mean value of the logical 1 level of the eye diagram. Bit Period - The reciprocal of the effective symbol rate. Eye Amplitude - A measure of the overall amplitude of the eye. It is based on the difference between the simple mean of the one level and the simple mean of the zero level. It is generally measured near the center of the eye. Eye Height - This is a measurement of the minimum vertical eye opening; basically, a determination of the signal to noise ratio. The measurement is made by taking the difference of the means of the one and zero levels then subtracting three times the standard deviation of each level. Eye Width - The eye width gives an indication of the total horizontal jitter in the signal. Like the eye height the measurement is statistical in nature. The horizontal histograms of two adjacent crossing points are used to determine the mean and standard deviations of crossing times. Three times the standard deviation of each distribution is subtracted from the difference of the two mean values. When enabled for the 10Base-T1S eye diagram, the eye height and eye width are displayed immediately below the eye diagram. Figure 4. Two vertical effects on the eye. The first pulse in the packet SSD field has noticeable vertical overshoot and droop, and Node ID #0 and ID #3 have differing zero levels. The vertical opening of the eye is affected by vertical related elements like additive noise and cross talk and other interfering signals as well as gain differences between devices on the bus. As an example of these vertical effects, consider the eye diagram of a 10Base-T1S packet shown in Figure 4. This eye diagram is using color persistence where the more frequent occurrences appear in the brighter colors. The violet trace (samples with a low occurrence rate) at the top has a high one level related to the first bit in the SSD field of Node ID #3. It is a zero and so appears as a double width segment. The other thing to notice is that the zero levels of the two nodes on the bus do not match exactly. The node with ID #0 has a higher zero level, which has the effect of decreasing the eye height. The measured eye height of 932 mV and eye width of 39.35 ns includes data from both nodes. The eye diagram shown is based on the full acquired signal and sees both nodes on the bus. The user can elect to generate the eye diagram for only the displayed zoom trace associated with the selected packet in the decode table, rather than the full acquisition. In this way, the source of any aberrations noted in the full acquisition can be isolated, first by selecting a specific packet, then shifting the zoom trace horizontally until the aberration disappears. The horizontal closure of the eye is the result of timing uncertainty. Timing jitter whether random, periodic or inter-symbol interference will tend to close the eye horizontally. Both nodes have common timing with no apparent horizontal differences. title: A blueprint for modern, connected in vivo programs
summary: Read Benchling’s blueprint for running a modern in vivo study, gathered from R&D scientists and IT leaders who shared their challenges and learnings.
body_text: It’s hard to run an efficient in vivo study. And often, they’re stuck using outdated communication and data management tools to do so. In vivo research is dynamic, complex, and tedious — teams need a modern approach to running these studies that supports the breakthroughs they’re pursuing every day. Our team at Benchling created this blueprint for building a modern in vivo program after hearing real pain points from hundreds of R&D scientists and IT leaders at Benchtalk 2022 , our annual biotechnology innovation summit. I hope their insights can power more efficient and effective in vivo research for your teams. These are the foundations that fueled Benchling In Vivo , part of our unified R&D platform used by 200,000+ scientists. To learn more, reach out to see a demo .

title: Os 3 principais desafios da gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista
summary: Práticas ESG, novos produtos, marketing favorável. Confira os desafios da gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista e como superá-los
body_text: Ainda que o consumo de cigarros seja alvo de vários debates por conta do impacto que causa na saúde dos seus usuários, não se pode negar que uma boa gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista é fundamental para garantir o bom funcionamento das empresas desse segmento que seguem ativas no Brasil. Sobre esse mercado, vale destacar que ele tem forte impacto na economia brasileira. Dados do SindiTabaco revelam que o nosso país ocupa a segunda posição no ranking dos maiores produtores mundiais de tabaco . Desde 1993, o Brasil se configura como o maior exportador desse produto para o mundo , sendo que mais de 85% do que é produzido aqui segue para o mercado internacional. No total são mais de 100 países abastecidos com o tabaco brasileiro, e apenas em 2021 as exportações desse setor chegaram a 464 mil toneladas. Mas para atender a esse mercado, bem como a produção de cigarros para venda ao consumidor final, a gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista enfrenta alguns importantes desafios. Esses obstáculos envolvem questões de ESG , oferta de novos produtos e marketing favorável. Siga a leitura deste artigo e confira agora, em detalhes, os pontos a serem superados para uma gestão de fornecedores na indústria de cigarros realmente eficiente. Os desafios da gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista Mesmo que a tendência seja de redução do número de fumantes no Brasil, cerca de 10% da população ainda consome cigarros, conforme apontado em uma matéria do site CNN Brasil . Para atender esse grupo de pessoas, a gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista precisa garantir o bom fluxo da produção, de modo que isso contribua para suprir o volume de vendas da empresa. Mas como dissemos, para chegar a esse resultado, é preciso passar por alguns obstáculos. Os três mais relevantes para esse segmento são: implementação de ESG na cadeia produtiva de tabaco; contribuição para a oferta de novos produtos contratação de parceiros para criação de estratégias positivas de marketing. Implementação de ESG na cadeia produtiva de tabaco Conforme apontamento da OMS, Organização Mundial da Saúde, citado em uma matéria do site G1 , a indústria tabagista causa sérios impactos ao meio ambiente. Além das substâncias químicas tóxicas usadas na fabricação de cigarros, o descarte do que sobra desse produto contribui para a poluição das praias, do mar e dos rios. Ainda segundo informações apresentadas na reportagem, a produção e o consumo de tabaco resultam na perda anual de, aproximadamente, 600 milhões de árvores, 200 mil hectares de terra, 22 bilhões de toneladas de água e a emissão de 84 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono na atmosfera. A fim de reduzir esse impacto, é fundamental que boas práticas de ESG sejam implementadas em toda a cadeia produtiva de tabaco, indo desde os processos de plantação, cultivo e colheita, até a fabricação e entrega do cigarro que será consumido pelo público final. Considerando esse cenário, uma das principais responsabilidades dos profissionais de gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista é garantir a sustentabilidade na cadeia de fornecedores (ESG) , por meio da identificação de provedores que sigam esse mesmo princípio. Somando o fomento à preservação do meio ambiente, essa prática também contribui para: melhorar a imagem da empresa; aumentar a transparência dos processos; chamar positivamente a atenção do público e de potenciais investidores. Contribuição para a oferta de novos produtos Uma das maiores empresas tabagistas do mundo, a Philip Morris, detentora de marcas como Harmony, L&M, Marlboro e Shelton, já anunciou que a meta é parar de vender cigarros. No Brasil, a companhia aguarda a aprovação da Anvisa para lançar um novo produto de tabaco sem combustão. Segundo relatado em uma matéria no site da Folha de S. Paulo , a proposta tem por objetivo a oferta de um dispositivo eletrônico que torna o consumo de tabaco menos nocivo. Esse novo modelo de negócio modifica a gestão de fornecedores em indústria tabagista, que precisarão identificar e qualificar provedores que oferecem insumos, matéria-prima e tecnologia compatíveis para a produção desse novo produto que será entregue nesse mercado. Contratação de fornecedores para criação de estratégias positivas de marketing Em meio a diversas campanhas antifumo, fazer marketing favorável à indústria tabagista é um verdadeiro desafio. Legalmente, campanhas publicitárias com o intuito de incentivar o consumo de cigarros são proibidas, restringindo totalmente o uso de peças publicitárias que normalmente podem ser utilizadas por outros setores. O segredo, portanto, é encontrar fornecedores especializados que entendam essas limitações e que sugiram abordagens paralelas que gerem efeito similar ao que seria colhido com estratégias de marketing tradicional. Para isso, a gestão de fornecedores com essa finalidade deve considerar pontos como: reais necessidades da empresa; capacidade de atendimento do provedor em questão; levantamento de riscos dessa contratação; qualificação adequada dos terceiros; realização de onboarding : avaliação de performance dos fornecedores. Como melhorar a gestão de fornecedores na indústria de cigarros? A melhor maneira de melhorar a gestão de fornecedores na indústria de cigarros é utilizando ferramentas apropriadas para essa tarefa . A Linkana é o primeiro e maior software de gestão de fornecedores em rede. Nossa base de dados de perfis compartilhados permite que compradores analisem fornecedores ativos e novos em alguns cliques. Com isso, criamos e geramos valor com insights de informações comerciais, de risco, qualidade e diversidade, utilizados em processos de cadastro, onboarding, sourcing e análise de spend. Entre as vantagens do uso dessa ferramenta estão: possibilidade de usar dados para basear tomadas de decisão; maior controle de riscos; automatização de processos; otimização da etapa de onboarding; identificação de fornecedores D&I. title: Flo Master’s 5 Minute Dynamic Warm-Up
summary: Before jumping into your workout be sure to prep your body by warming up first. Avoid injuries and setbacks in just 5 minutes with this dynamic warm-up.
body_text: One of the keys to long-term longevity with fitness involves taking care of your body. All too often we feel pressed on time and jump directly into our workouts to try and save time. In the end, this direct path usually leads to injury and setbacks, inevitably leading to lost time. The truth is, a good five minutes of warming up will properly prep your body for training. FightCamp Trainer Flo Master designed this quick dynamic warm-up to allow your body to fully warm up, avoid injury, and let you get the most out of your workout. Flo performs this routine before he does any kickboxing, jiu-jitsu, or boxing work. Flo’s 5 Minute Dynamic Warm-up Routine A-Skips (30 seconds) Similar to marching in place, the A-skip has you add a little bounce to your march as if you were to skip in place Focus on controlled motion and raising the knee up above hip-height Arms should be at 90 degrees swinging the opposite arm up as the opposite knee is lifted Focus on breathing in through your nose and out through your mouth Continue skipping for 30 seconds Side Shuffle (30 seconds) Start off in an athletic stance, feet shoulder-width apart Begin to shuffle to your right for three shuffles Pause and shuffle back to your left for three shuffles Your chest should remain forward as you shuffle side to side Do not cross your legs while shuffling Continue shuffling for 30 seconds High Knees (30 seconds) Similar to the A-skip, high knees remove the slight bounce and have you repetitively perform the knee drives at a higher tempo Focus on controlled motion and raising the knee up above hip-height Arms should be at 90 degrees swinging the opposite arm up as the opposite knee is lifted Focus on breathing in through your nose and out through your mouth Continue high knees for 30 seconds High Knee Shuffles (30 seconds) This movement combines high knees with side shuffling Perform three shuffles to your right, pause on one foot for a second, then perform three shuffles to your left Focus on controlled
